standard: Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) — 15 U.S.C. 6501-6505; 16 CFR Part 312
source: FTC Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule (curated minor-protection corpus)

entries.title: COPPA applicability — under-13 operators
entries.body: COPPA imposes requirements on operators of websites or online services directed to children under 13, and on operators with actual knowledge they are collecting personal information online from a child under 13. An 'operator' includes anyone who collects, uses, or discloses personal information from children, including AI tutoring platforms that ingest chats, voice, or work product.

entries.title: Verifiable parental consent required
entries.body: Before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from a child under 13, operators must obtain verifiable parental consent. The FTC has approved multiple methods (e.g., credit-card backed, signed consent forms, video identity checks) and the 2025 amendments add new approved methods.

entries.title: Personal information includes persistent identifiers, biometrics, voice
entries.body: Under COPPA, 'personal information' covers name, address, email, screen/online contact, persistent identifiers (cookies, device IDs), geolocation, photos, voice recordings, and biometric identifiers. AI tutors that transcribe or analyze a child's voice or typing patterns must treat those as personal information.

entries.title: School authorization substitutes for parental consent (education context)
entries.body: Schools may authorize collection of a child's personal information for a legitimate educational purpose in lieu of parental consent. The 2025 COPPA amendments move to codify a 'school authorization' exception for ed-tech, consistent with FTC guidance that schools act in loco parentis for classroom use.

entries.title: Parental review, deletion, and refusal rights
entries.body: Parents have the right to review the personal information collected from their child, to refuse further collection or use, and to have it deleted. AI tutor products should provide a parent-facing dashboard to exercise these rights.

entries.title: Data security, retention, and deletion obligations
entries.body: Operators must maintain reasonable security, confidentiality, and integrity of children's personal information and retain it only as long as necessary. The 2025 amendments strengthen information-security, deletion, and retention protocols and require periodic review.

entries.title: 2025 COPPA Rule amendments — effective dates
entries.body: The FTC's 2025 final amendments to the COPPA Rule were effective June 23, 2025, with a general compliance date of April 22, 2026 (except a few provisions). They add a 'mixed-audience' definition, broaden 'personal information' (government IDs, biometrics), and update notices and consent methods. Some ed-tech/school-role amendments were deferred pending FERPA changes.

entries.title: Ed-tech/school-role amendments deferred (enforce per existing guidance)
entries.body: In the 2025 final rule the FTC did NOT finalize proposed ed-tech and school-authorization amendments, to avoid conflict with pending FERPA revisions. It continues to enforce COPPA in the ed-tech context under existing guidance; AI tutor vendors should still follow the school-authorization and data-minimization posture.

entries.title: Mixed-audience services default posture
entries.body: The 2025 amendments add a 'mixed audience' website/service definition to clarify audience composition. Services that are not purely child-directed but reach children should default to treating users as children absent reliable age assurance, an important posture for general-purpose AI tutors.

entries.title: AI tutors as COPPA operators
entries.body: An AI tutoring tool that collects chats, voice, drawings, or assessment data from users known or likely under 13 is a COPPA operator. It must gate collection behind verifiable parental consent (or valid school authorization) and minimize retention of minor data.

entries.title: FTC-approved COPPA Safe Harbor programs
entries.body: The FTC approves Safe Harbor programs under which members following the program's guidelines are deemed in compliance. Joining a safe harbor can structure an AI tutor's compliance program but does not eliminate the underlying obligations.

entries.title: FTC enforcement and civil penalties
entries.body: The FTC enforces COPPA and may seek civil penalties for each violation, plus injunctive relief and refunds. FTC actions have targeted ed-tech and children's apps (e.g., Edmodo, Chegg, Epic Games) for unlawful collection and disclosure of minor data.
